sentences.text: Morag is fifteen and she works weekends at the enclosure in the summer and she is very good with the visitors, everybody says so.
She tells them the true and cheerful things.
That reindeer hooves spread in summer and harden in winter.
That they are the only deer where the females keep antlers through the winter, which is why every Christmas card in Britain is wrong.
That this herd came from Sweden in 1952 and that the man who brought them was called Mikel Utsi and that the first three arrived by boat.
She tells them that reindeer can see ultraviolet, which is genuinely the best fact on the hill and which stops a group of eight-year-olds dead every single time.
Snow reflects UV and lichen absorbs it, and so does fur, and so does urine, which means that a landscape that looks blank white to a person is, to a reindeer, covered in writing.
She does not tell them about the bull.

It is not a secret and there is no rule about it and if a visitor asked her directly she would answer honestly, and one man did, in 2026, who turned out to know a great deal about herds in Norway, and she talked to him for forty minutes.

He said that the same argument was going on in three places in Finnmark and that nobody there had twenty-one years of dates either, because the people who know are herders and herders write down what they need and nothing else.
He gave her an email address and she has not used it, and it is in the front of her mother's notebook on a piece of card.
The reason she does not tell them is that it does not work as a nice fact.
Every other thing she says on that hill can be said in a cheerful voice to a family with a four-year-old.
*He comes down and it snows within thirty hours* is a wonderful one — it is the best one she has — and it was true for eighteen years and she cannot say it any more without saying the rest.

And the rest is: he still comes down, and he is still right about the plateau, and the plateau is not what it was, and the notebook her mother keeps with the flapjack recipe in it is now a record of something nobody set out to record.
Her mother has kept it up.
Twenty-third of November 2025, thirty-one days.
She writes it in the same handwriting in among the feed orders and does not comment.
Morag has asked her twice whether she is going to send it to anybody.

Her mother says she is a herder and not a scientist and that the notebook is for the feed, and that if somebody wants it after she is finished with it they are welcome to it, and that in the meantime there are animals to see to.
Morag has a copy.
She made it at fourteen, over about six evenings, photographing every page on her phone, and she has it in two places and one of them is not in that house.
She did not ask permission and she did not hide it either.
Her mother came in halfway through the third evening, looked at what she was doing, said nothing whatsoever, and put the kettle on.
That is the only conversation the two of them have ever had about whether the notebook matters, and Morag thinks it was a fairly complete one.
